articles.author: Jonathan Jones
articles.title: Cat’s whiskers: Nan Goldin proves that she’s the greatest US artist since Warhol – review
articles.description: Hayward Gallery, London The photographer finds echoes of Caravaggio and Greek myth in her erotic images, while her disturbing animal montages show that while humans can be beautiful, we are far from innocent It’s the dirty realism of Nan Goldin ’s images, her unfazed photography of the rough seams of spontaneous, dangerous lives, that enables her to create a film of such unlikely ambition as Stendhal Syndrome. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen. She infects you with it in a ravishing work housed in what looks like a bronze yurt entered via a vaulted corridor. If this seems ostentatious, the film justifies the ceremony. A montage of sensual images teems with Goldin’s uniquely raw, immediate feel for the human presence as she photographs her friends, mostly in the nude, legs wrapped round each other, or lying in a swoon, or touching themselves, or bathing together. Here is the unfeigned, honest impact her work has had since she first put her world viscerally on camera in her early photo series The Ballad of Sexual Dependency . But there’s a difference. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jack Seale
articles.title: The Witch Farm review – this creepy tale is laugh-out-loud funny … without meaning to be
articles.description: Danny Robins follows up his Uncanny paranormal documentary about a Welsh farm with this drama. Subtle it isn’t – it’s bedlam from the get-go and at times it’s so OTT it’s unwittingly hilarious A lot of strange and scary stuff happened in 1989 at Heol Fanog, a lonely farmhouse at the foot of Bannau Brycheiniog (formerly known as the Brecon Beacons). English artist Bill Rich and his pregnant Welsh partner, Liz, moved there with Bill’s teenage son to begin again, replacing the complexity of urban life with the still silence of the remote countryside. But their new start became a protracted nightmare when they experienced what seemed to be supernatural phenomena – and the Heol Fanog ghosts would keep appearing to the Rich family for another seven years. The case – nicknamed the “Welsh Amityville” for its similarities to the US’s most famous instance of reported paranormal activity – has long haunted Danny Robins, presenter of the podcast and BBC Two TV series Uncanny, in which he investigates claims of interactions with the undead. Heol Fanog stands out because of the sheer number of eerie events, the length of time across which they took place, and the multiple witnesses: if you can explain this, what about that? Or that? Or, oh my God, THAT? Continue reading...

articles.author: Editorial
articles.title: The Guardian view on Serbia’s new political era: a generational opportunity must not be wasted | Editorial
articles.description: Brussels must find ways to show concrete support for a new government that will genuinely share the EU’s democratic values Following the extraordinary election that swept Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government from power, Serbia’s new political era has begun. Outside the National Assembly in Belgrade last week, large crowds celebrated as MPs from the victorious Student List movement were sworn in. Doctors, lawyers and academics put forward as candidates by the youthful protesters, who took on Mr Vučić, are now tasked with running an expectant country. Their defining challenge will be to restore trust and democratic legitimacy in a nation that, under Mr Vučić’s bullying rule, plunged towards the bottom of Europe’s corruption rankings. Legal action has already begun against figures accused of illicitly profiting from the previous regime, while the new parliament’s elected speaker – a professor and organic farmer – called for the restoration of dignity and tolerance to its proceedings in his first address. Ensuring academic and media independence, and reforming the security services, which acted as the former president’s authoritarian enforcers on the streets, will be urgent priorities. articles.title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial
articles.description: The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents. Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments . The inspection that led to the downgrading of her primary school to “inadequate” was judged to have contributed to her death. In its 2024 manifesto, Labour promised to replace one-word labels with more nuanced overviews of schools’ performance. Continue reading...

articles.description: Clincal psychotherapist Gareth Strangemore-Jones responds to an article on persistent assumptions about masculinity Sarah Blaffer Hrdy’s research offers an important challenge to one of our most persistent assumptions about masculinity: that nurturing is somehow contrary to male nature ( Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so, 17 November ). As a clinical psychotherapist, I find the most compelling implication is not simply that children benefit from involved fathers, but that fathers themselves may change through the experience of caring. We often imagine psychological development as a process in which attitudes must change before behaviour follows. Yet caregiving may work in both directions. Repeated experiences of responding to another person’s vulnerability can engage and potentially strengthen the biological and psychological systems involved in emotional responsiveness, attachment and cooperation. articles.description: Orford church, Suffolk Performed in the venue where Noye’s Fludde premiered and based on the same text, this festive new work shines with exuberant young performers, distinctive singalongs, lustrous designs and the spirit of mucking in When Benjamin Britten wrote Noye’s Fludde, he essentially invented community opera. articles.title: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause
articles.description: Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con? ‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live , billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee. The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. ( Fungi are big news in the menopause wellness world, often touted as an answer to brain fog. Though at best the scientific jury is still out, Ocado searches for lion’s mane mushrooms more than quadrupled after an episode of Clarkson’s Farm in which Jeremy Clarkson’s partner, Lisa Hogan, persuaded him to grow them to make supplements, claiming that “everyone who’s anyone” is on them.) On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics? In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned. Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. articles.author: Laura Barton
articles.title: ‘He’s open and affable – I avoid being recognised like the plague’: Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon on celebrity, friendship and their trip to the Arctic circle
articles.description: The northern lights, fine food, Melvyn Bragg impersonations – The Trip has landed in Scandinavia. We take in the sights with its stars, as they ruminate on ageing, activism and the best car to take a nap in Morning in Valldal, and in the pale September light, the Juvet Landskapshotell stands quite still amid mountains, pines and yellowing birch. In the hotel dining room, Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon are taking breakfast; coffee and muesli and compote spread out before them as they settle into a discussion of the playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen, and their enduring infatuations with much younger women. “When Ibsen was 60, he fell in love with a teenager called Emilie,” Brydon says. “Can you imagine doing that?” Coogan swallows his muesli: “I can imagine it …” The conversation shifts, taking in the persecuted genius of Galileo, a short exhortation on the subject of Palestine, and how the aurora borealis has just been spotted in the skies above Great Yarmouth. After a time, Brydon falls into an extended impersonation of Melvyn Bragg presenting In Our Time. “Can you expand on that?” he barks at Coogan. “Expand … Expand … Expand.” The edges of Coogan’s mouth begin to flicker. articles.author: John Harris
articles.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
articles.description: Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be. All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict . But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of sexism. But one of the tragedies of Labour’s 18 long years of exile from power and the climactic defeat of organised labour in the miners’ strike was the fact that they opened the way for the wholesale reinvention of work and watershed developments that we seem to be only just waking up to. articles.title: ‘Harsh to be under her thumb’: Pitchfork’s Ryan Schreiber on selling to Condé Nast and Anna Wintour
articles.description: He shocked the industry when he ‘sold out’ to corporate media in 2015. For the first time since leaving, he opens up about his new life as an out gay man and why he quit On the early November day that I met Pitchfork founder Ryan Schreiber in New York City, the website he created is all that anyone on my timeline can talk about, again. Today, it’s thanks to a freshly dug-up tweet from Jon Ossoff, the newly re-elected Georgia senator, who sincerely wrote in 2012: “Looking forward to your writeup of the new @imaginedragons album.” It’s an all-timer, up there with Phoebe Bridgers saying that she thinks about the site’s review of Jet’s second album (a video of a monkey pissing in its own mouth) once a day, and Halsey wishing that the Pitchfork office, which is on the site of the 9/11 attacks in New York, would “collapse already”. The joke in Ossoff’s case is that Pitchfork would not be caught dead praising the purveyors of stomp clap radio rock; a 2021 review characterized the band’s music as “emotions fired out of a T-shirt cannon”. articles.title: ‘I do a really good version of AC/DC’s Highway to Hell, which throws people’: Sharleen Spiteri’s honest playlist
articles.description: The Texas singer was fascinated by Elvis Costello as a kid and admires Nancy Sinatra’s sass and strength, but which of her own songs changed her life? The first song I fell in love with My mum gave me an old Dansette record player and a pile of albums. I must have been eight or 10, with my younger sister Corinne, getting butterflies to These Boots Are Made for Walkin’ by Nancy Sinatra. Years later, I read that she was told to sing it with a much more provocative attitude. You can hear the sass and the strength. Maybe that’s where my whole “don’t fuck with me” thing came from. The song I do at karaoke Give me any Marvin Gaye song, like You’re All I Need to Get By, and I’m all over it, but I’d normally pull someone up to duet with me. Continue reading...

articles.description: As MPs discuss the menace of ‘high-control religious groups’, I welcome the political attention – but survivors of this abuse deserve real action Rachael Reign is the founder of Surviving Universal UK Britain is confronting its cult problem. articles.author: Arifa Akbar
articles.title: Lend them your ears! Julius Caesar is staged with just four actors – and a great big gong
articles.description: Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, London This truncated, candlelit version makes use of skilful percussion to occasionally fill in for oration but loses some of the play’s beauty and power Any modern reformulation of Julius Caesar may inevitably be compared with Phyllida Lloyd’s innovative, all-female 2012 production, now revived by the Royal Shakespeare Company , which reimagined the tragedy as a play-within-a-play in a women’s prison. This reworked version, adapted and directed by Joe Hill-Gibbins, does not match its depth and originality but certainly does something different. It is performed at 90 minutes straight-through with just four actors who take on the central roles of conspirators Cassius (Natey Jones) and Brutus (Caoilfhionn Dunne) alongside Mark Antony (Adam Gillen) and Caesar (Kate Duchêne, who also plays the soothsayer and Octavius). It is not as gimmicky as you may think. Continue reading...
